gallery.filename: Burke Museum totem poles 01.jpg
gallery.title: File:Burke Museum totem poles 01.jpg
gallery.description:
Totem poles outside Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture, University of Washington, Seattle, Washington.

These are 20th century replicas of 19th century totem poles. The pole on the left is a Tsimshian memorial pole (original carved circa 1880, replica carved 1970 by Bill Holm). The pole on the right is a Haida house front pole (original carved circa 1870, replica carved 1969 by Bill Holm).
categories: Native American art in the Burke Museum of Natural History and Culture

gallery.filename: Flauta de carrizo Carrizo (acatl) Pech flute Honduras.JPG
gallery.title: File:Flauta de carrizo Carrizo (acatl) Pech flute Honduras.JPG
gallery.description: Made by Pech craftman Hernan Martínez Escobar, co-author of Los Pech de Honduras, who lives in Moradel, Trujillo, Colon. Made of carrizo, a bamboo like plant which only grows above 1,500 feet.  A special kind of black wax made by the same bees which make miel de blanco, the best kind of medicinal honey and who only live in forests is also needed to make this kind of flute. Although this is a Pech flute, similar flutes were made in Honduras by the Miskito Indians, the Tawahka Indians, and the Lenca indians.  The Pech also previously made jaguar bone flutes. One flute is supposed to sound like pavon and the other the pajuil, both rainforest birds. The bee, the carrizo, the pavon, the pajuil, and music that sounds like the pavon and pajuil are all in danger of extinction. This was the first example of a Pech carrizo flute made in 20 years. This flute is in the collection of the Burke Museum, along with the other instruments needed to play at  a Pech religious ceremony maracas and a Pech drum.  The mountains above the Pech villages of Olancho are called the Sierra de Agalta, which comes from acalta, in Nahua (agalta in Nicarao dialect of Nahua) or carrizal, a place of a lot of carrizo cane.

gallery.filename: Canasta carrizo chorti Guatemala.JPG
gallery.title: File:Canasta carrizo chorti Guatemala.JPG
gallery.description: This basket of Carrizo, (acalt in Nahua) a bamboo like cane found only above 1,500 feet was made by the Maya Chortis of Guatemala, but was bought in Copan Ruinas, Honduras, where the Maya Chortis do not have any carrizo on their land. In Honduras carrizo baskets are commonly made by the Lencas such as in Chinacla, La Paz. Carrizo is currently very scarce in Honduras as above 1,500 feet is also the preferred elevation for growing arábica coffee. This size basket (una tortillera) is generally used in Honduras to hold tortillas wrapped in a White cotton cloth, often embroidered. Larger baskets can hold up to 40 lbs. of bananas or rosquillas for sale. Carrizo baskets which held approximately 4 pounds (una medida) were the only form of measurement of goods sold in interior markets in Honduras still in the 1940's according to anthropologist Doris Z. Stone. This Carrizo basket is in the collection of the Burke Museum, University of Washington.

gallery.filename: Copal chorti copan ruinas Honduras.JPG
gallery.title: File:Copal chorti copan ruinas Honduras.JPG
gallery.description: In Honduras, Copal incense is burnt by the Maya Chorti Indians, the Lenca Indians, and the Garífunas including those of Colon. This copal was probably made in Guatemala, but was sold in the market of Copan ruinas, Honduras, as the Maya Chortis of Honduras do not have enough forest lands to meet their needs of copal. The Honduran Maya Chortis form it into coins to burn it for ceremonias of which they maintain a signficant number. The Garífunas mix it with other herbs to keep away evil spirits for ceremonies and some times burn it alone to keep their houses smelling fresh. Copal is made of the resin of a tree. When Aztec King Moctezuma I attacked Honduras in the Post Classic period to make it pay tribute according to Fray Torquemada he wanted them to pay tribute in the form of Green stones, Green feathers, gold, cacao, animal skins, and resins which probably included liquidámbar,rubber, pine, balsalm, and copal. This copal is in the collection of the Burke Museum, University of Washington.
